output.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
output.body:
Scope creep is not really a build problem. It is a decision problem.

For a small business, the cleanest boundary is simple: pick one recurring workflow, define the measure, and write the scope before any build starts. In the Bareni diagnostic, that means asking: what is the one repeatable workflow that costs time or creates risk, and how will we know it is better?

That question matters because it keeps the work inspectable. If the current workflow is invoice logging, then the pilot is about invoice logging. If someone wants customer replies, lead follow-up, and reporting in the same pass, that is not one workflow. It is three.

The practical control is to write a short scope check in advance. One workflow. One owner. One measurable outcome. One approval boundary. If a new request appears during the build, pause and decide whether it belongs in this pilot or the next one.

That is not being difficult. It is how you keep a small automation investment from turning into a loose pile of “while you’re in there” requests.

The next step is to name one weekly workflow, in plain English, and write down the success measure you already use today. That becomes the input for the diagnostic and the proposal.
